description: The maintainer's adjacency ruling on issue #944's sibling question: a newline separates exactly like a space -- always, everywhere. Adjacency is whitespace-agnostic; a newline is insignificant to the GRAMMAR, not invisible to the LEXER. This is a NARROWING, and the mechanism is why it was invisible: a newline token's `end` IS the next line's column 1, so once a container skipped the newline the following `[` tested as adjacent to what preceded it -- a skipped newline MANUFACTURED an adjacency the source never had. Measured against the built parser at `0277d5ff` before the fix, `[ :nums` + newline + `[1] ]` read `[1]` as a SELECTOR on `:nums` and printed `[20]`, while the spaced `[ :nums [1] ]` read a second element and printed `[[10 20 30] [1]]`. The two spellings now agree, and this fixture proves it as a VALUE rather than as a diagnostic, which is why a list literal is the container: both spellings execute in it. The parenthesized and top-level containers are malformed in their spaced spelling for reasons unrelated to adjacency (an arity error at the top level), so their agreement is pinned in the companion `core-language/check/a-newline-separates-like-a-space-when-malformed` instead. The glued spelling is printed too and must NOT match the other two: without it this fixture would still pass if adjacency stopped working altogether, since all three spellings would then agree on the non-selector reading. The final row is the regression this direction had to avoid -- a newline after a comprehension header selects the long body form (`spec/grammar.md:34`), so the `[` binds as a BODY; a narrowing can only make the `[` less likely to bind, so it is strictly more protected than before, but that is asserted rather than assumed.
